Source: EnterpriseRAG/github_public

Connector: github_public

1. * * provider rate - limit escalation ignored : * * apis commonly increase ` retry - after ` values on repeated 429 responses ( e. g., openai, azure, anthropic ). the router ignores this escalation, retrying with the initial short delay. 2. * * request storms against rate - limited apis : * * by retrying 12× faster than requested, the router floods the provider during rate - limit windows, potentially prolonging the rate - limit period or triggering harder throttling / account suspension. 3. * * triggers for single - deployment setups : * * the backoff calculation is used when ` _ time _ to _ sleep _ before _ retry `

    "title": "[Bug]: Router ignores Retry-After (instant retry) for multi-deployment model groups sharing one rate-limited upstream",
    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/github_public",
    "content": "{\n  \"artifact_type\": \"issue\",\n  \"author\": \"segevfiner\",\n  \"body\": \"## Check for existing issues\\n- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.\\n\\n## What happened?\\n\\n`Router._time_to_sleep_before_retry` only honors the upstream `Retry-After` header when a model group has a **single** deployment. As soon as a model group has **more than one** deployment (and there is \\u22651 \\\"healthy\\\" deployment), it returns `0` and retries **instantly**, discarding `Retry-After`:\\n\\n```python\\n# litellm/router.py :: _time_to_sleep_before_retry\\n## base case - single deployment\\nif all_deployments is not None and len(all_deployments) == 1:\\n    pass                       # -> reads Retry-After from the exception headers\\nelif (\\n    healthy_deployments is not None\\n    and isinstance(healthy_deployments, list)\\n    and len(healthy_deployments) > 0\\n):\\n    return 0                   # -> instant retry, Retry-After ignored\\n```\\n\\nThe assumption is that with multiple deployments the router can immediately fail over to a *different, healthy* deployment. But when the deployments in the group all point to the **same upstream / share the same rate-limit or token quota**, they are all throttled at once. The instant retries then just hammer the throttled upstream and burn through `num_retries` in a fraction of a second, never waiting the time the provider explicitly asked for.\\n\\nConcretely, an upstream returning `429` with `Retry-After: 15`:\\n- **Single-deployment group** \\u2192 retries at ~15s intervals (correct).\\n- **Multi-deployment group (same upstream)** \\u2192 retries ~instantly (~0.1\\u20130.3s apart), all fail, request errors out well within the 15s window.\\n\\n### Expected\\n`Retry-After` should be honored regardless of deployment count when the retry lands on a deployment/upstream that advertised it \\u2014 or at least there should be a way to opt in (e.g. respect `Retry-After` before instant-failover, or a router flag). Instant-failover should not silently override an explicit provider back-off signal, since sibling deployments frequently share the same throttled backend.\\n\\n## Steps to Reproduce\\n\\n1. Save this mock upstream that always returns `429` + `Retry-After: 15` and logs the gap between hits, and run it (`python3 mock_429.py`):\\n\\n   ```python\\n   # mock_429.py\\n   import json, time\\n   from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer\\n   RA = 15\\n   last = {\\\"t\\\": None}\\n   class H(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):\\n       def do_POST(self):\\n           now = time.time()\\n           gap = \\\"-\\\" if last[\\\"t\\\"] is None else f\\\"{now-last['t']:.2f}s\\\"\\n           last[\\\"t\\\"] = now\\n           self.rfile.read(int(self.headers.get(\\\"content-length\\\", 0)))\\n           print(f\\\"[mock] HIT {time.strftime('%H:%M:%S')} gap={gap}\\\", flush=True)\\n           body = json.dumps({\\\"error\\\": {\\\"message\\\": \\\"rate limited\\\", \\\"type\\\": \\\"rate_limit_error\\\"}}).encode()\\n           self.send_response(429)\\n           self.send_header(\\\"content-type\\\", \\\"application/json\\\")\\n           self.send_header(\\\"content-length\\\", str(len(body)))\\n           self.send_header(\\\"retry-after\\\", str(RA))\\n           self.end_headers()\\n           self.wfile.write(body)\\n       def log_message(self, *a): pass\\n   ThreadingHTTPServer((\\\"127.0.0.1\\\", 8130), H).serve_forever()\\n   ```\\n\\n2. `config.yaml` \\u2014 a **single** model group `long` with **two distinct deployments** (different `model_id`) that both hit the same throttled upstream. `allowed_fails` is raised so cooldown doesn't pull the deployments out of rotation before the retry timing can be observed:\\n\\n   ```yaml\\n   general_settings:\\n     master_key: sk-mp\\n   litellm_settings:\\n     num_retries: 3\\n     allowed_fails: 100\\n   model_list:\\n     - model_name: long\\n       litellm_params: { model: custom_openai/gpt-x, api_base: http://127.0.0.1:8130, api_key: sk-a }\\n     - model_name: long\\n       litellm_params: { model: custom_openai/gpt-x, api_base: http://127.0.0.1:8130, api_key: sk-b }\\n   ```\\n\\n   > Note: the two entries must be **distinct** deployments (here, different `api_key` \\u2192 different `model_id`). Two byte-identical entries collapse to one `model_id` and get deduped/co-cooled, which masks the timing behavior.\\n\\n3. `litellm --config config.yaml` and send one request:\\n\\n   ```bash\\n   curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions \\\\\\n     -H \\\"Authorization: Bearer sk-mp\\\" -H \\\"content-type: application/json\\\" \\\\\\n     -d '{\\\"model\\\":\\\"long\\\",\\\"messages\\\":[{\\\"role\\\":\\\"user\\\",\\\"content\\\":\\\"hi\\\"}]}'\\n   ```\\n\\n4. Observe the mock's hit gaps: all retries fire **~0.01\\u20130.02s** apart (instant), never waiting the advertised 15s. Now collapse to a **single** deployment (delete the `sk-b` entry) and repeat \\u2192 gaps become **~15s** (Retry-After honored). Same upstream and `Retry-After` in both cases; the only difference is deployment count within the group.\\n\\n## Relevant log output\\n\\n```\\n# Two distinct deployments in the 'long' group (Retry-After: 15 IGNORED):\\n[mock] HIT 18:13:50 gap=-\\n[mock] HIT 18:13:50 gap=0.02s\\n[mock] HIT 18:13:50 gap=0.01s\\n[mock] HIT 18:13:50 gap=0.01s\\n\\n# Single deployment 'long' (Retry-After: 15 honored):\\n[mock] HIT 18:03:27 gap=-\\n[mock] HIT 18:03:43 gap=15.79s\\n[mock] HIT 18:03:58 gap=15.74s\\n```\\n\\n## What part of LiteLLM is this about?\\nProxy (Router \\u2014 `router.py` `_time_to_sleep_before_retry`)\\n\\n## What LiteLLM version are you on?\\nv1.90.0 (also reproduced on v1.88.1)\",\n  \"changed_files\": [],\n  \"closed_at\": \"\",\n  \"comments_count\": 0,\n  \"commit_summaries\": [],\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"body\",\n    \"conversation\",\n    \"reviews\",\n    \"commit_summaries\",\n    \"changed_files\",\n    \"timeline\"\n  ],\n  \"conversation\": [],\n  \"created_at\": \"2026-07-23T15:44:25Z\",\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"gh_e1b669559933513cb6bd51e864cf1ff3\",\n  \"draft\": false,\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"llm translation\",\n    \"proxy\"\n  ],\n  \"merged_at\": \"\",\n  \"milestone\": \"\",\n  \"number\": 34399,\n  \"owner\": \"BerriAI\",\n  \"provenance\": [\n    \"GitHub REST and GraphQL API; document.title: [Bug]: Router ignores Retry-After (instant retry) for multi-deployment model groups sharing one rate-limited upstream
document.content:
{
  "artifact_type": "issue",
  "author": "segevfiner",
  "body": "## Check for existing issues
- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

## What happened?

`Router._time_to_sleep_before_retry` only honors the upstream `Retry-After` header when a model group has a **single** deployment. As soon as a model group has **more than one** deployment (and there is ≥1 "healthy" deployment), it returns `0` and retries **instantly**, discarding `Retry-After`:

```python
# litellm/router.py :: _time_to_sleep_before_retry
## base case - single deployment
if all_deployments is not None and len(all_deployments) == 1:
    pass                       # -> reads Retry-After from the exception headers
elif (
    healthy_deployments is not None
    and isinstance(healthy_deployments, list)
    and len(healthy_deployments) > 0
):
    return 0                   # -> instant retry, Retry-After ignored
```

The assumption is that with multiple deployments the router can immediately fail over to a *different, healthy* deployment. But when the deployments in the group all point to the **same upstream / share the same rate-limit or token quota**, they are all throttled at once. The instant retries then just hammer the throttled upstream and burn through `num_retries` in a fraction of a second, never waiting the time the provider explicitly asked for.

Concretely, an upstream returning `429` with `Retry-After: 15`:
- **Single-deployment group** → retries at ~15s intervals (correct).
- **Multi-deployment group (same upstream)** → retries ~instantly (~0.1–0.3s apart), all fail, request errors out well within the 15s window.

### Expected
`Retry-After` should be honored regardless of deployment count when the retry lands on a deployment/upstream that advertised it — or at least there should be a way to opt in (e.g. respect `Retry-After` before instant-failover, or a router flag). Instant-failover should not silently override an explicit provider back-off signal, since sibling deployments frequently share the same throttled backend.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Save this mock upstream that always returns `429` + `Retry-After: 15` and logs the gap between hits, and run it (`python3 mock_429.py`):

   ```python
   # mock_429.py
   import json, time
   from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer
   RA = 15
   last = {"t": None}
   class H(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
       def do_POST(self):
           now = time.time()
           gap = "-" if last["t"] is None else f"{now-last['t']:.2f}s"
           last["t"] = now
           self.rfile.read(int(self.headers.get("content-length", 0)))
           print(f"[mock] HIT {time.strftime('%H:%M:%S')} gap={gap}", flush=True)
           body = json.dumps({"error": {"message": "rate limited", "type": "rate_limit_error"}}).encode()
           self.send_response(429)
           self.send_header("content-type", "application/json")
           self.send_header("content-length", str(len(body)))
           self.send_header("retry-after", str(RA))
           self.end_headers()
           self.wfile.write(body)
       def log_message(self, *a): pass
   ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 8130), H).serve_forever()
   ```

2. `config.yaml` — a **single** model group `long` with **two distinct deployments** (different `model_id`) that both hit the same throttled upstream. `allowed_fails` is raised so cooldown doesn't pull the deployments out of rotation before the retry timing can be observed:

   ```yaml
   general_settings:
     master_key: sk-mp
   litellm_settings:
     num_retries: 3
     allowed_fails: 100
   model_list:
     - model_name: long
       litellm_params: { model: custom_openai/gpt-x, api_base: http://127.0.0.1:8130, api_key: sk-a }
     - model_name: long
       litellm_params: { model: custom_openai/gpt-x, api_base: http://127.0.0.1:8130, api_key: sk-b }
   ```

   > Note: the two entries must be **distinct** deployments (here, different `api_key` → different `model_id`). Two byte-identical entries collapse to one `model_id` and get deduped/co-cooled, which masks the timing behavior.

3. `litellm --config config.yaml` and send one request:

   ```bash
   curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-mp" -H "content-type: application/json" \
     -d '{"model":"long","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}]}'
   ```

4. Observe the mock's hit gaps: all retries fire **~0.01–0.02s** apart (instant), never waiting the advertised 15s. Now collapse to a **single** deployment (delete the `sk-b` entry) and repeat → gaps become **~15s** (Retry-After honored). Same upstream and `Retry-After` in both cases; the only difference is deployment count within the group.

## Relevant log output

```
# Two distinct deployments in the 'long' group (Retry-After: 15 IGNORED):
[mock] HIT 18:13:50 gap=-
[mock] HIT 18:13:50 gap=0.02s
[mock] HIT 18:13:50 gap=0.01s
[mock] HIT 18:13:50 gap=0.01s

# Single deployment 'long' (Retry-After: 15 honored):
[mock] HIT 18:03:27 gap=-
[mock] HIT 18:03:43 gap=15.79s
[mock] HIT 18:03:58 gap=15.74s
```

## What part of LiteLLM is this about?
Proxy (Router — `router.py` `_time_to_sleep_before_retry`)

## What LiteLLM version are you on?
v1.90.0 (also reproduced on v1.88.1)",

{
  "channel": "incidents",
  "thread_ts": "1719532100",
  "first_message_ts": "1719532100",
  "last_message_ts": "1719532487",
  "participants": [
    "incident-bot",
    "alice (oncall)",
    "ben (sre)",
    "carla (plat-lead)",
    "devon (customer-success)",
    "eric (infra)",
    "frank (eng)"
  ],
  "messages": "incident-bot: SEV2 - spike in 5xx and latency starting ~1719532000. Smart-routing fallback is triggering cross-region failover and we're seeing request duplication. Alert: https://ops.redwood.internal/alerts/INC-9812 :rotating_light:

alice (oncall): on it. paging ben + carla. assigning PD to ben now.

ben (sre): ack. seeing error rate ~12% on /v1/generate from region-eu and sudden CPU spikes on region-us replicas. graphs: p95 latency doubled, outgoing request count to us replicas ~= incoming * 2.

carla (plat-lead): hypothesis: failover policy is misconfigured to fanout to multiple compatible variants/regions instead of single fallback. combined with aggressive client retry policy -> thundering herd. any recent policy deploys?

frank (eng): I pushed a routing-policy tweak yesterday (experiment: multi-variant fallback) to reduce model mismatch errors. might be related.

ben (sre): logs show client retry headers like `Retry-After: 0` and exponential retries for 429/503. clients retry immediately -> our smart-routing fires failover to region-us; because of the policy change, it also sends to a variant in us-ssd, effectively doubling attempts.

eric (infra): scaling is reacting but slower. we temporarily hit admission limits on the us pool and started rejecting, which fed back to clients -> more retries.

alice (oncall): impact? which customers affected? devon can you pull support queue and customer-facing signals?

devon (customer-success): seeing 8 open tickets referencing "slow responses" and 2 on L3 customers reporting degraded throughput for embeddings. letting sales know. preparing customer comms draft.

ben (sre): immediate mitigation plan: 1) rollback last routing-policy experiment (disable multi-variant fanout) 2) apply a short ephem rate-limit on cross-region failover traffic 3) instruct clients to honor Retry-After and set recommended jitter/backoff.

carla (plat-lead): agree. frank can you revert the policy flag quickly? If we can't revert, apply a patch to change fallback_mode -> single_hop.

frank (eng): doing revert now. CLI: `curl -X PATCH https://console.redwood.internal/api/policies/route-983 -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -d '{"fallback_mode":"single_hop","fanout":false}'`


deploy-bot: routing-policy route-983: change applied by frank at 1719532224.

ben (sre): applying transient rate-limit on proxy: `rlimit set --route /v1/generate --match header:X-Region-Fallback --rate 200r/s`

eric (infra): rate limit in place and we bumped us replica admission to +20% to absorb steady-state.

alice (oncall): ben, can you confirm whether duplicates stopped?

ben (sre): metrics: outgoing requests to us replicas now approx equal incoming. 5xx rate falling from 12% -> 1.8% in last 3m. latency trending down. marking as mitigated. :white_check_mark:

devon (customer-success): sending provisional customer note: "We've mitigated an incident causing increased latency and errors for some requests. Root cause: routing policy change combined with aggressive client retries. We'll follow up with permanent fixes and recommended client backoff guidance."

carla (plat-lead): please open follow-up tickets: - postmortem (owner: ben) - client-backoff doc update (owner: frank) - routing-policy safe-deploy checks (owner: carla) - customer RCA + comms (owner: devon)

frank (eng): creating PR to add a gating test to policy deploys to detect fanout configs. snippet I ran locally that triggered the issue: ```json
{
  "id":"route-983",
  "fallback_mode":"multi_variant",
  "fanout": true,
  "compatible_variants":["gpt-medium","gpt-quant-lite"]
}
```

ben (sre): note for postmortem: interplay of client retry loops + policy fanout = traffic amplification. mitigation effective but temporary. we should add server-side dedup or prefer single-hop fallback by default.

alice (oncall): closing incident channel. will handover to ben/carla for postmortem. thanks all.

incident-bot: INCIDENT INC-9812 status -> mitigated at 1719532487. PagerDuty: resolved.
",
  "title_field_name": "channel",
  "content_field_names": [
    "messages"
  ],
  "dataset_doc_uuid": "dsid_e517587192f0436899fc48bf180a4dc1"
}

    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/github_public",
    "content": "{\n  \"artifact_type\": \"pull_request\",\n  \"author\": \"unfitcoder101\",\n  \"body\": \"Fixes #34399\\r\\n\\r\\n## Problem\\r\\n`_time_to_sleep_before_retry` unconditionally returns 0 (instant retry) whenever a model group has more than one healthy deployment, discarding any `Retry-After` header the upstream provider sent. Sibling deployments frequently share the same throttled upstream (e.g. two deployments with different `api_key`s pointing at the same backend), so instant retries hammer the throttled endpoint and burn through `num_retries` well within the provider's advertised backoff window.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Why opt-in, not a default change\\r\\nThe existing instant-retry-on-healthy-deployments behavior is deliberate and locked in by an existing test (`test_timeout_for_rate_limit_error_with_healthy_deployments`), which explicitly asserts `timeout == 0` in this scenario. Rather than changing default behavior, this adds an opt-in `respect_retry_after_with_multiple_deployments` flag (default `False`) to `Router.__init__`. Default behavior is completely unchanged and verified unchanged by a new test.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Fix\\r\\nWhen `respect_retry_after_with_multiple_deployments=True`, an explicit `Retry-After` header is honored even with healthy sibling deployments present.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Tests\\r\\n- Default behavior unchanged (instant retry, even with `Retry-After` present)\\r\\n- Opt-in honors `Retry-After` with multiple deployments\\r\\n- Opt-in still allows instant retry when no `Retry-After` header is present\\r\\n\\r\\nAll existing router retry tests pass except one pre-existing, unrelated environmental failure (missing `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` locally), confirmed identical with and without this change via `git stash`.\",\n  \"changed_files\": [\n    \"litellm/router.py (+25, -6, MODIFIED)\",\n    \"tests/litellm/test_router_retry_backoff_headers.py (+135, -0, MODIFIED)\"\n  ],\n  \"closed_at\": \"\",\n  \"comments_count\": 0,\n  \"commit_summaries\": [\n    \"2026-07-23T17:51:09Z 713d484f5402: feat(router): add opt-in flag to honor Retry-After with multiple depl\\u2026\",\n    \"2026-07-23T19:33:07Z 196bee02b8e1: chore: trigger fresh CI run after docs fix\",\n    \"2026-07-24T18:07:43Z e8e3f4d03733: chore: retrigger CI after full local verification\"\n  ],\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"body\",\n    \"conversation\",\n    \"reviews\",\n    \"commit_summaries\",\n    \"changed_files\",\n    \"timeline\"\n  ],\n  \"conversation\": [],\n  \"created_at\": \"2026-07-23T17:52:17Z\",\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"gh_1aa9d68730e805e44b2245e53d0e6a7a\",\n  \"draft\": true,\n  \"labels\": [],\n  \"merged_at\": \"\",\n  \"milestone\": \"\",\n  \"number\": 34408,\n  \"owner\": \"BerriAI\",\n  \"provenance\": [\n    \"GitHub REST and GraphQL API; document.title: feat(router): add opt-in flag to honor Retry-After with multiple deployments
document.content:
{
  "artifact_type": "pull_request",
  "author": "unfitcoder101",
  "body": "Fixes #34399\r\n\r\n## Problem\r\n`_time_to_sleep_before_retry` unconditionally returns 0 (instant retry) whenever a model group has more than one healthy deployment, discarding any `Retry-After` header the upstream provider sent. Sibling deployments frequently share the same throttled upstream (e.g. two deployments with different `api_key`s pointing at the same backend), so instant retries hammer the throttled endpoint and burn through `num_retries` well within the provider's advertised backoff window.\r\n\r\n## Why opt-in, not a default change\r\nThe existing instant-retry-on-healthy-deployments behavior is deliberate and locked in by an existing test (`test_timeout_for_rate_limit_error_with_healthy_deployments`), which explicitly asserts `timeout == 0` in this scenario. Rather than changing default behavior, this adds an opt-in `respect_retry_after_with_multiple_deployments` flag (default `False`) to `Router.__init__`. Default behavior is completely unchanged and verified unchanged by a new test.\r\n\r\n## Fix\r\nWhen `respect_retry_after_with_multiple_deployments=True`, an explicit `Retry-After` header is honored even with healthy sibling deployments present.\r\n\r\n## Tests\r\n- Default behavior unchanged (instant retry, even with `Retry-After` present)\r\n- Opt-in honors `Retry-After` with multiple deployments\r\n- Opt-in still allows instant retry when no `Retry-After` header is present\r\n\r\nAll existing router retry tests pass except one pre-existing, unrelated environmental failure (missing `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` locally), confirmed identical with and without this change via `git stash`.",

{
  "document": {
    "id": "dsid_ca42a8f18d784c879c5a6fcfe3a484c0",
    "path": "/knowledge/company/sources/confluence/customer-success-and-support/known-issues-and-workarounds/overload-errors-and-retry-guidance.json",
    "title": "Hosted API overload errors: support guidance, retry/backoff, and escalation",
    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/confluence",
    "content": "{\n  \"title\": \"Hosted API overload errors: support guidance, retry/backoff, and escalation\",\n  \"space\": \"customer-success-and-support\",\n  \"author\": \"Dev Patel\",\n  \"owner_team\": \"customer-success\",\n  \"status\": \"published\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2025-11-10\",\n  \"last_updated\": \"2025-12-05\",\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"hosted-api\",\n    \"overload\",\n    \"load-shedding\",\n    \"circuit-breaker\",\n    \"retry-guidance\",\n    \"support-playbook\",\n    \"error-codes\"\n  ],\n  \"confidentiality\": \"internal\",\n  \"reviewers\": [\n    \"Rafael Mendes\",\n    \"Christine Wong\",\n    \"Nikhil Sharma\",\n    \"Elliot Price\"\n  ],\n  \"related_pages\": [\n    \"sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-014-hosted-overload-error-taxonomy.json\",\n    \"sources/confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/runbooks/hosted-overload-circuit-breaker-runbook.json\",\n    \"sources/confluence/eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets/hosted-api-slo-overload-exceptions-and-budget-policy.json\",\n    \"sources/confluence/eng-developer-experience/docs-site/hosted-api-overload-errors-doc-update.json\"\n  ],\n  \"content\": \"## Purpose\\nThis page helps Support/CS respond to customer reports of new \\u201coverload protection\\u201d errors (circuit breakers + load shedding) on Redwood Hosted API.\\n\\nGoals:\\n- Explain what the customer is seeing (stable semantics vs ambiguous timeouts/5xx).\\n- Provide canonical retry/backoff guidance to prevent retry storms.\\n- Show how to interpret correlation IDs so Engineering can quickly trace requests.\\n- Define escalation criteria and the minimum information to collect.\\n\\n## What changed (customer-facing)\\nWhen the platform is saturated (GPU capacity, scheduler backlog, downstream dependency brownout), Redwood may reject requests *early* and predictably rather than allowing them to time out or generate random 5xx.\\n\\nCustomers may now see:\\n- **429** responses for admission / quota / per-tenant caps.\\n- **503** responses when a regional/model circuit breaker is open or the system is actively shedding load.\\n\\nThese responses:\\n- Include stable **error codes** and a machine-readable JSON payload.\\n- Typically include a **Retry-After** header to indicate safe retry timing.\\n- Include Redwood request/correlation IDs for tracing.\\n\\n## Quick triage checklist (Support)\\n1) Confirm this is an overload-protection response (see \\u201cHow to recognize\\u201d below).\\n2) Verify the customer is following recommended retry/backoff (or advise them to change).\\n3) Collect required debug info (IDs, time window, region/model, response headers).\\n4) Determine if this is expected transient overload vs a bug/misconfig (missing Retry-After, incorrect status mapping, fallback not triggering).\\n5) Escalate to Eng Oncall when criteria are met (see \\u201cWhen to escalate\\u201d).\\n\\n## How to recognize overload-protection responses\\n### Common HTTP statuses\\n- **429 Too Many Requests**\\n  - Used for admission controls such as per-tenant concurrency caps, token buckets, or tier limits.\\n  - Usually safe to retry with backoff if Retry-After is provided.\\n\\n- **503 Service Unavailable**\\n  - Used when the platform is overloaded at the regional/model level (breaker open) or actively shedding load to protect SLOs.\\n  - Usually safe to retry with backoff and/or reduce load. May persist until capacity recovers.\\n\\n### Expected headers (may vary by route)\\n- **Retry-After**: integer seconds is preferred (e.g., `Retry-After: 2`).\\n- **x-redwood-request-id**: unique ID for a single request attempt.\\n- **x-redwood-correlation-id**: groups related attempts across services (gateway \\u2192 routing \\u2192 runtime). Some clients/logs only show one of these; either is helpful.\\n\\nIf the response is 429/503 *and* includes a Redwood overload error code in the JSON body, treat it as overload protection.\\n\\n## Error payload: what customers see\\nOverload errors are additive and JSON-compatible with existing response parsing.\\n\\nTypical shape (example):\\n- `error.type`: `overload_error` (or `rate_limit_error` in some cases)\\n- `error.code`: stable machine code\\n- `error.message`: human-readable\\n- `error.request_id`: mirrors `x-redwood-request-id` where available\\n- `error.correlation_id`: mirrors `x-redwood-correlation-id` where available\\n\\nExample snippet (illustrative only):\\n{\\n  \\\"error\\\": {\\n    \\\"type\\\": \\\"overload_error\\\",\\n    \\\"code\\\": \\\"BREAKER_OPEN\\\",\\n    \\\"message\\\": \\\"The service is temporarily overloaded. Please retry after the specified delay.\\\",\\n    \\\"request_id\\\": \\\"req_01J9...\\\",\\n    \\\"correlation_id\\\": \\\"corr_01J9...\\\"\\n  }\\n}\\n\\n## Canonical mapping: status \\u2192 meaning \\u2192 what we tell customers\\nUse this table to drive consistent customer guidance.\\n\\n| HTTP | Typical meaning | What Support should say | Customer action |\\n|------|------------------|--------------------------|-----------------|\\n| 429 | Admission control / rate limiting / tier cap hit | \\u201cYour request was rejected to protect system stability. This is not a model failure; it indicates you are sending requests faster than the current allowed rate/concurrency.\\u201d | Respect Retry-After; implement exponential backoff + jitter; reduce concurrency; consider batching; if persistent, discuss tier/capacity options. |\\n| 503 | Regional/model breaker open or load shedding | \\u201cRedwood is temporarily overloaded in the requested region/model. We are rejecting early to avoid timeouts and protect overall reliability.\\u201d | Respect Retry-After; backoff + jitter; optionally route to another region/model if configured; reduce max_tokens/streaming concurrency; retry with bounded attempts. |\\n\\nNotes:\\n- If the customer reports **timeouts** with no JSON error, treat as a separate issue (possible client/network or upstream timeouts) and escalate based on impact.\\n- If the customer gets **5xx** without the overload payload, collect details; it may be an unrelated incident.\\n\\n## Retry & backoff guidance (what we should recommend)\\n### Golden rules\\n- **Always respect Retry-After** when provided.\\n- **Use exponential backoff with jitter**; do not retry immediately.\\n- **Cap retries** to avoid amplifying overload.\\n- **Reduce concurrency** rather than increasing it during overload.\\n- Prefer **idempotency keys** for safe retries on non-streaming requests.\\n\\n### Recommended algorithm (support-approved)\\nIf `Retry-After` is present:\\n- Sleep `Retry-After` seconds, then retry.\\n\\nIf `Retry-After` is missing:\\n- Backoff schedule suggestion: 0.5s, 1s, 2s, 4s, then stop (max 4 retries), each with \\u00b120\\u201340% jitter.\\n\\nBounds:\\n- Maximum total retry time budget: **~10\\u201320 seconds** for interactive apps, **~60 seconds** for batch jobs.\\n- Maximum concurrent retries: keep to a small fraction of steady-state concurrency (e.g., 10\\u201320%).\\n\\n### Streaming-specific guidance\\nStreaming workloads can worsen overload if clients open many concurrent streams.\\n- Recommend **lower streaming concurrency** during peak periods.\\n- If the customer can tolerate it, recommend **shorter outputs** (reduce `max_tokens`) and/or **shorter prompts**.\\n- If a stream fails mid-response with an overload error on reconnect attempts, advise them to back off and resume with a bounded number of attempts.\\n\\n### What NOT to recommend\\n- \\u201cJust retry in a tight loop.\\u201d\\n- \\u201cRetry immediately with the same concurrency.\\u201d\\n- \\u201cSpin up many parallel retries to get through.\\u201d\\n\\n## How to interpret and use correlation IDs\\n### Which IDs to ask for\\nAsk the customer for (in order of preference):\\n1) `x-redwood-correlation-id` (best for cross-service tracing)\\n2) `x-redwood-request-id` (single request attempt)\\n3) Timestamp + region + model + route if IDs are not available\\n\\n### Where customers can find them\\n- Response headers in their HTTP client.\\n- SDK exception fields (Python/TypeScript SDKs surface request IDs; newer versions surface correlation IDs when present).\\n- Their application logs if they log response headers.\\n\\n### How Support should use them internally\\n- Paste the ID(s) into the internal log search / tracing tool.\\n- Capture:\\n  - the **error.code**\\n  - the **route** (e.g., `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/responses`, embeddings endpoint)\\n  - the **region** (requested + served)\\n  - whether **Retry-After** was present and its value\\n\\nIf Support cannot access dashboards/tracing, escalate with the IDs and all details in the escalation template below.\\n\\n## Common customer questions + approved responses\\n### \\u201cIs Redwood down?\\u201d\\nApproved response:\\n\\u201cNot necessarily. These errors indicate Redwood is protecting service reliability during temporary saturation in a specific region/model. We reject early with clear retry guidance to avoid timeouts and degraded performance. Please follow the Retry-After header and exponential backoff. If the issue persists beyond a short window, share correlation IDs and we\\u2019ll investigate.\\u201d\\n\\n### \\u201cWhy am I seeing 503 if this is overload?\\u201d\\nApproved response:\\n\\u201c503 is used when the platform is temporarily unable to serve the request due to load shedding or an open circuit breaker. It\\u2019s a deliberate, controlled response (with stable error codes) to prevent cascading failures and long tail latency.\\u201d\\n\\n### \\u201cShould I fail over to another model/region?\\u201d\\nGuidance:\\n- If they have **fallback routing configured** (Dedicated/enterprise Hosted tiers or configured routing policies), yes\\u2014recommend they enable/verify it.\\n- Otherwise, advise them to implement client-side fallback only if they can validate output compatibility and safety.\\n\\n### \\u201cCan you increase my limits?\\u201d\\nGuidance:\\n- Confirm whether they are hitting **429** (likely limit-related) vs **503** (regional/model saturation).\\n- If 429 is persistent at normal traffic levels, route to CS for capacity/tier discussion.\\n- If 503 is persistent, treat as reliability issue and escalate to Eng.\\n\\n## Known issues (Support-facing)\\n1) **Retry-After header missing on some overload responses**\\n- Symptom: Customer receives 429/503 overload payload but no Retry-After.\\n- Workaround: Recommend exponential backoff with jitter as above.\\n- Action: Escalate if reproducible; include route + correlation IDs.\\n\\n2) **Fallback model not triggering as expected**\\n- Symptom: Customer has configured fallback but still sees repeated 503 without failover.\\n- Workaround: Customer can temporarily specify an alternate model/region explicitly (if acceptable) while we investigate.\\n- Action: Escalate; include tenant ID, configured fallback policy (what they intended), and correlation IDs.\\n\\n3) **Customer interprets 503 as \\u201cplatform outage\\u201d**\\n- Guidance: Use the approved response language; direct them to Retry-After and backoff guidance.\\n\\n## When to escalate to Engineering (Eng Oncall / SRE)\\nEscalate immediately if any of the following are true:\\n- **Enterprise customer** reporting sustained overload errors impacting production.\\n- Overload errors persist for **>15 minutes** with correct backoff behavior.\\n- **No Retry-After** observed on multiple responses for the same route/region/model.\\n- Suspected **misclassification** (e.g., 500s that should be 429/503 overload, or overload codes returned with 200/stream interruptions).\\n- **Fallback routing configured** but not activating.\\n- Customer reports sharp regression (new errors) coincident with a canary/rollout and provides IDs.\\n\\n## Escalation template (copy/paste)\\nSubject: Hosted API overload errors \\u2013 customer impact\\n\\n- Customer / tenant: \\n- Tier: (Self-serve Hosted / Enterprise Hosted / Dedicated)\\n- Primary route(s): (e.g., /v1/chat/completions)\\n- Model(s): \\n- Region(s): requested / observed\\n- Time window (with timezone): \\n- Error HTTP status: 429 / 503\\n- Error code(s) from body: \\n- Retry-After present? value(s): \\n- x-redwood-correlation-id(s): \\n- x-redwood-request-id(s): \\n- Customer retry behavior (describe): \\n- Business impact: (prod down / degraded / batch delay)\\n- Attachments: sample responses (headers + body), client logs\\n\\n## Internal-only: where to look (for Support with access)\\n- Overload dashboards: shed rate, breaker-open rate, queue depth, saturation signals by region/model.\\n- Incident channels: #eng-oncall, #incidents (look for breaker announcements).\\n- Runbook: \\u201cHosted overload / circuit breaker runbook\\u201d (linked above).\\n\\n## Revision history\\n- 2025-11-10: Initial publication for overload error rollout (Support readiness).\\n- 2025-12-05: Updated retry guidance; clarified correlation IDs and escalation thresholds.\\n\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"content\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_ca42a8f18d784c879c5a6fcfe3a484c0\"\n}",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Hosted API overload errors: support guidance, retry/backoff, and escalation\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/confluence\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/confluence/customer-success-and-support/known-issues-and-workarounds/overload-errors-and-retry-guidance.json\nConnector: confluence\nWorkspace: customer-success-and-support\n\n##tries : keep to a small fraction of steady - state concurrency ( e. g., 10 – 20 % ). # # # streaming - specific guidance streaming workloads can worsen overload if clients open many concurrent streams. - recommend * * lower streaming concurrency * * during peak periods. - if the customer can tolerate it, recommend * * shorter outputs * * ( reduce ` max _ tokens ` ) and / or * * shorter prompts * *. - if a stream fails mid - response with an overload error on reconnect attempts, advise them to back off and resume with a bounded number of attempts.",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Hosted API overload errors: support guidance, retry/backoff, and escalation\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/confluence\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/confluence/customer-success-and-support/known-issues-and-workarounds/overload-errors-and-retry-guidance.json\nConnector: confluence\nWorkspace: customer-success-and-support\n\nan overload error on reconnect attempts, advise them to back off and resume with a bounded number of attempts. # # # what not to recommend - “ just retry in a tight loop. ” - “ retry immediately with the same concurrency. ” - “ spin up many parallel retries to get through. ” # # how to interpret and use correlation ids # # # which ids to ask for ask the customer for ( in order of preference ) : 1 ) ` x - redwood - correlation - id ` ( best for cross - service tracing ) 2 ) ` x - redwood - request - id ` ( single request attempt ) 3 ) timestamp + region + model + route if ids are not available",

  "author": "Dev Patel",
  "owner_team": "customer-success",
  "status": "published",
  "created_at": "2025-11-10",
  "last_updated": "2025-12-05",
  "labels": [
    "hosted-api",
    "overload",
    "load-shedding",
    "circuit-breaker",
    "retry-guidance",
    "support-playbook",
    "error-codes"
  ],
  "confidentiality": "internal",
  "reviewers": [
    "Rafael Mendes",
    "Christine Wong",
    "Nikhil Sharma",
    "Elliot Price"
  ],
  "related_pages": [
    "sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-014-hosted-overload-error-taxonomy.json",
    "sources/confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/runbooks/hosted-overload-circuit-breaker-runbook.json",
    "sources/confluence/eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets/hosted-api-slo-overload-exceptions-and-budget-policy.json",
    "sources/confluence/eng-developer-experience/docs-site/hosted-api-overload-errors-doc-update.json"
  ],
  "content": "## Purpose
This page helps Support/CS respond to customer reports of new “overload protection” errors (circuit breakers + load shedding) on Redwood Hosted API.

Goals:
- Explain what the customer is seeing (stable semantics vs ambiguous timeouts/5xx).
- Provide canonical retry/backoff guidance to prevent retry storms.
- Show how to interpret correlation IDs so Engineering can quickly trace requests.
- Define escalation criteria and the minimum information to collect.

## What changed (customer-facing)
When the platform is saturated (GPU capacity, scheduler backlog, downstream dependency brownout), Redwood may reject requests *early* and predictably rather than allowing them to time out or generate random 5xx.

Customers may now see:
- **429** responses for admission / quota / per-tenant caps.
- **503** responses when a regional/model circuit breaker is open or the system is actively shedding load.

These responses:
- Include stable **error codes** and a machine-readable JSON payload.
- Typically include a **Retry-After** header to indicate safe retry timing.
- Include Redwood request/correlation IDs for tracing.

## Quick triage checklist (Support)
1) Confirm this is an overload-protection response (see “How to recognize” below).
2) Verify the customer is following recommended retry/backoff (or advise them to change).
3) Collect required debug info (IDs, time window, region/model, response headers).
4) Determine if this is expected transient overload vs a bug/misconfig (missing Retry-After, incorrect status mapping, fallback not triggering).
5) Escalate to Eng Oncall when criteria are met (see “When to escalate”).

## How to recognize overload-protection responses
### Common HTTP statuses
- **429 Too Many Requests**
  - Used for admission controls such as per-tenant concurrency caps, token buckets, or tier limits.
  - Usually safe to retry with backoff if Retry-After is provided.

- **503 Service Unavailable**
  - Used when the platform is overloaded at the regional/model level (breaker open) or actively shedding load to protect SLOs.
  - Usually safe to retry with backoff and/or reduce load. May persist until capacity recovers.

### Expected headers (may vary by route)
- **Retry-After**: integer seconds is preferred (e.g., `Retry-After: 2`).
- **x-redwood-request-id**: unique ID for a single request attempt.
- **x-redwood-correlation-id**: groups related attempts across services (gateway → routing → runtime). Some clients/logs only show one of these; either is helpful.

If the response is 429/503 *and* includes a Redwood overload error code in the JSON body, treat it as overload protection.

## Error payload: what customers see
Overload errors are additive and JSON-compatible with existing response parsing.

Typical shape (example):
- `error.type`: `overload_error` (or `rate_limit_error` in some cases)
- `error.code`: stable machine code
- `error.message`: human-readable
- `error.request_id`: mirrors `x-redwood-request-id` where available
- `error.correlation_id`: mirrors `x-redwood-correlation-id` where available

Example snippet (illustrative only):
{
  "error": {
    "type": "overload_error",

    "message": "The service is temporarily overloaded. Please retry after the specified delay.",
    "request_id": "req_01J9...",

## Canonical mapping: status → meaning → what we tell customers
Use this table to drive consistent customer guidance.

| HTTP | Typical meaning | What Support should say | Customer action |
|------|------------------|--------------------------|-----------------|
| 429 | Admission control / rate limiting / tier cap hit | “Your request was rejected to protect system stability. This is not a model failure; it indicates you are sending requests faster than the current allowed rate/concurrency.” | Respect Retry-After; implement exponential backoff + jitter; reduce concurrency; consider batching; if persistent, discuss tier/capacity options. |
| 503 | Regional/model breaker open or load shedding | “Redwood is temporarily overloaded in the requested region/model. We are rejecting early to avoid timeouts and protect overall reliability.” | Respect Retry-After; backoff + jitter; optionally route to another region/model if configured; reduce max_tokens/streaming concurrency; retry with bounded attempts. |

Notes:
- If the customer reports **timeouts** with no JSON error, treat as a separate issue (possible client/network or upstream timeouts) and escalate based on impact.
- If the customer gets **5xx** without the overload payload, collect details; it may be an unrelated incident.

## Retry & backoff guidance (what we should recommend)
### Golden rules
- **Always respect Retry-After** when provided.
- **Use exponential backoff with jitter**; do not retry immediately.
- **Cap retries** to avoid amplifying overload.
- **Reduce concurrency** rather than increasing it during overload.
- Prefer **idempotency keys** for safe retries on non-streaming requests.

### Recommended algorithm (support-approved)
If `Retry-After` is present:
- Sleep `Retry-After` seconds, then retry.

If `Retry-After` is missing:
- Backoff schedule suggestion: 0.5s, 1s, 2s, 4s, then stop (max 4 retries), each with ±20–40% jitter.

Bounds:
- Maximum total retry time budget: **~10–20 seconds** for interactive apps, **~60 seconds** for batch jobs.
- Maximum concurrent retries: keep to a small fraction of steady-state concurrency (e.g., 10–20%).

### Streaming-specific guidance
Streaming workloads can worsen overload if clients open many concurrent streams.
- Recommend **lower streaming concurrency** during peak periods.
- If the customer can tolerate it, recommend **shorter outputs** (reduce `max_tokens`) and/or **shorter prompts**.
- If a stream fails mid-response with an overload error on reconnect attempts, advise them to back off and resume with a bounded number of attempts.

### What NOT to recommend
- “Just retry in a tight loop.”
- “Retry immediately with the same concurrency.”
- “Spin up many parallel retries to get through.”

## How to interpret and use correlation IDs
### Which IDs to ask for
Ask the customer for (in order of preference):
1) `x-redwood-correlation-id` (best for cross-service tracing)
2) `x-redwood-request-id` (single request attempt)
3) Timestamp + region + model + route if IDs are not available

### Where customers can find them
- Response headers in their HTTP client.
- SDK exception fields (Python/TypeScript SDKs surface request IDs; newer versions surface correlation IDs when present).
- Their application logs if they log response headers.

### How Support should use them internally
- Paste the ID(s) into the internal log search / tracing tool.
- Capture:
  - the **error.code**
  - the **route** (e.g., `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/responses`, embeddings endpoint)
  - the **region** (requested + served)
  - whether **Retry-After** was present and its value

If Support cannot access dashboards/tracing, escalate with the IDs and all details in the escalation template below.

## Common customer questions + approved responses
### “Is Redwood down?”
Approved response:
“Not necessarily. These errors indicate Redwood is protecting service reliability during temporary saturation in a specific region/model. We reject early with clear retry guidance to avoid timeouts and degraded performance. Please follow the Retry-After header and exponential backoff. If the issue persists beyond a short window, share correlation IDs and we’ll investigate.”

### “Why am I seeing 503 if this is overload?”
Approved response:
“503 is used when the platform is temporarily unable to serve the request due to load shedding or an open circuit breaker. It’s a deliberate, controlled response (with stable error codes) to prevent cascading failures and long tail latency.”

### “Should I fail over to another model/region?”
Guidance:
- If they have **fallback routing configured** (Dedicated/enterprise Hosted tiers or configured routing policies), yes—recommend they enable/verify it.
- Otherwise, advise them to implement client-side fallback only if they can validate output compatibility and safety.

### “Can you increase my limits?”
Guidance:
- Confirm whether they are hitting **429** (likely limit-related) vs **503** (regional/model saturation).
- If 429 is persistent at normal traffic levels, route to CS for capacity/tier discussion.
- If 503 is persistent, treat as reliability issue and escalate to Eng.

## Known issues (Support-facing)
1) **Retry-After header missing on some overload responses**
- Symptom: Customer receives 429/503 overload payload but no Retry-After.
- Workaround: Recommend exponential backoff with jitter as above.
- Action: Escalate if reproducible; include route + correlation IDs.

2) **Fallback model not triggering as expected**
- Symptom: Customer has configured fallback but still sees repeated 503 without failover.
- Workaround: Customer can temporarily specify an alternate model/region explicitly (if acceptable) while we investigate.
- Action: Escalate; include tenant ID, configured fallback policy (what they intended), and correlation IDs.

3) **Customer interprets 503 as “platform outage”**
- Guidance: Use the approved response language; direct them to Retry-After and backoff guidance.

## When to escalate to Engineering (Eng Oncall / SRE)
Escalate immediately if any of the following are true:
- **Enterprise customer** reporting sustained overload errors impacting production.
- Overload errors persist for **>15 minutes** with correct backoff behavior.
- **No Retry-After** observed on multiple responses for the same route/region/model.
- Suspected **misclassification** (e.g., 500s that should be 429/503 overload, or overload codes returned with 200/stream interruptions).
- **Fallback routing configured** but not activating.
- Customer reports sharp regression (new errors) coincident with a canary/rollout and provides IDs.

## Escalation template (copy/paste)
Subject: Hosted API overload errors – customer impact

- Customer / tenant: 
- Tier: (Self-serve Hosted / Enterprise Hosted / Dedicated)
- Primary route(s): (e.g., /v1/chat/completions)
- Model(s): 
- Region(s): requested / observed
- Time window (with timezone): 
- Error HTTP status: 429 / 503
- Error code(s) from body: 
- Retry-After present? value(s): 
- x-redwood-correlation-id(s): 
- x-redwood-request-id(s): 
- Customer retry behavior (describe): 
- Business impact: (prod down / degraded / batch delay)
- Attachments: sample responses (headers + body), client logs

## Internal-only: where to look (for Support with access)
- Overload dashboards: shed rate, breaker-open rate, queue depth, saturation signals by region/model.
- Incident channels: #eng-oncall, #incidents (look for breaker announcements).
- Runbook: “Hosted overload / circuit breaker runbook” (linked above).

## Revision history
- 2025-11-10: Initial publication for overload error rollout (Support readiness).
- 2025-12-05: Updated retry guidance; clarified correlation IDs and escalation thresholds.

- Pinned source: `litellm@8f86c87f8e065343af6e74e0823ab8a8276b9528`

`Router._time_to_sleep_before_retry` honors an upstream `Retry-After` header
for a single deployment but returns zero immediately when another healthy
deployment exists. That assumes deployments have independent limits. In
practice, several deployments can share one upstream quota, so instant retries
hammer the throttled service and exhaust the retry budget before its backoff
window ends.

Acceptance criteria:

1. A focused test represents two deployments sharing a rate-limited upstream.
2. An explicit upstream backoff is not silently discarded merely because a
   sibling deployment is healthy.
3. Immediate failover remains possible when no upstream backoff applies.
4. The change states the precedence between provider backoff and router retry
   policy.

def _get_retry_after_from_exception_header(
    response_headers: Optional[httpx.Headers] = None,
):
    """
    Reimplementation of openai's calculate retry after, since that one can't be imported.
    https://github.com/openai/openai-python/blob/af67cfab4210d8e497c05390ce14f39105c77519/src/openai/_base_client.py#L631
    """
    try:
        import email  # openai import

        # About the Retry-After header: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Retry-After
        #
        # <http-date>". See https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Retry-After#syntax for
        # details.
        if response_headers is not None:
            retry_header = response_headers.get("retry-after")
            try:
                retry_after = int(retry_header)
            except Exception:
                retry_date_tuple = email.utils.parsedate_tz(retry_header)  # type: ignore
                if retry_date_tuple is None:
                    retry_after = -1
                else:
                    retry_date = email.utils.mktime_tz(retry_date_tuple)  # type: ignore
                    retry_after = int(retry_date - time.time())
        else:
            retry_after = -1

        return retry_after

    except Exception:
        retry_after = -1


def _calculate_retry_after(
    remaining_retries: int,
    max_retries: int,
    response_headers: Optional[httpx.Headers] = None,
    min_timeout: int = 0,
) -> Union[float, int]:
    retry_after = _get_retry_after_from_exception_header(response_headers)

    # Add some jitter (default JITTER is 0.75 - so upto 0.75s)
    jitter = JITTER * random.random()

    # If the API asks us to wait a certain amount of time (and it's a reasonable amount), just do what it says.
    if retry_after is not None and 0 < retry_after <= 60:
        return retry_after + jitter

    # Calculate exponential backoff
    num_retries = max_retries - remaining_retries
    sleep_seconds = INITIAL_RETRY_DELAY * pow(2.0, num_retries)

    # Make sure sleep_seconds is boxed between min_timeout and MAX_RETRY_DELAY
    sleep_seconds = max(sleep_seconds, min_timeout)
    sleep_seconds = min(sleep_seconds, MAX_RETRY_DELAY)

    return sleep_seconds + jitter

# LiteLLM #34399 review

## Contract

When an upstream response carries a valid `Retry-After` delay (greater than zero and no more than LiteLLM's existing 60-second safety bound), that provider backoff takes precedence over the router's immediate retry to a healthy sibling deployment. When no valid upstream backoff applies, a healthy sibling deployment still permits immediate failover.

## Evidence

- Issue snapshot: `/knowledge/company/sources/github_public/BerriAI/litellm/issues/34399.json` (`gh_e1b669559933513cb6bd51e864cf1ff3`). Two distinct deployments can share one upstream quota; instant retries discard `Retry-After` and exhaust the retry budget.
- Curated source snapshot: `/code/upstream-issues/litellm-34399.md` (`enterprise_2034a8245bcfb88af6beb9e8`), pinned at `8f86c87f8e065343af6e74e0823ab8a8276b9528`.
- Throttling incident: `/knowledge/company/sources/slack/incidents/1719532100-client-backoff-misconfig-failover-burst.json` (`dsid_e517587192f0436899fc48bf180a4dc1`). Retry amplification and multi-variant fanout increased pressure; mitigation included honoring Retry-After and limiting fallback fanout.
- Support guidance: `/knowledge/company/sources/confluence/customer-success-and-support/known-issues-and-workarounds/overload-errors-and-retry-guidance.json` (`dsid_ca42a8f18d784c879c5a6fcfe3a484c0`). For 429 responses, respect Retry-After, use backoff/jitter, and reduce concurrency.
- Related upstream proposal snapshot: `/knowledge/company/sources/github_public/BerriAI/litellm/pulls/34408.json` (`gh_1aa9d68730e805e44b2245e53d0e6a7a`).

## Change

- `/code/litellm/litellm/router.py`: extract the provider delay before the healthy-deployment shortcut and allow the shortcut only when the existing Retry-After parser finds no valid bounded delay.
- `/code/litellm/tests/local_testing/test_router_retries.py`: update the existing multi-deployment expectation; add a deterministic two-deployment/shared-upstream regression; add a no-header case proving immediate failover remains intact.

## Validation

- `python3 -m py_compile litellm/router.py tests/local_testing/test_router_retries.py`: passed.
- Focused pytest command attempted:
  `python3 -m pytest tests/local_testing/test_router_retries.py -k 'timeout_for_rate_limit_error_with_healthy_deployments or shared_upstream_retry_after or healthy_deployment_failover_is_immediate' -q`
  but the isolated image has no pytest installed.
- An offline attempt to provision pytest with uv also failed because pytest is absent from the local package cache. No network or paid provider was used.
- Branch diff contains only the router source and retry test file.

## Operational consequence

Shared-quota deployment groups will wait for a valid provider-advertised delay instead of consuming all retries immediately. Independent deployments retain zero-delay failover when the error has no valid Retry-After. The existing 60-second validity ceiling and jitter behavior are unchanged.

## Rollback

Revert the two changed files (or remove the Retry-After guard from the healthy-deployment shortcut and the associated regression cases). This restores unconditional immediate failover whenever a healthy sibling exists.

Owner: Kaitlyn Nguyen
Tags: litellm, retry-after, failover, rate-limit, router

## Summary

In Router._time_to_sleep_before_retry, parse provider response headers before applying the healthy-deployment fast path. A valid bounded Retry-After (>0 and <=60 seconds under LiteLLM's existing policy) takes precedence because sibling deployments may share an upstream quota. If no valid upstream backoff exists, preserve zero-delay failover to a healthy sibling. Regression coverage must include two distinct deployments with different keys sharing one api_base plus a no-Retry-After control.
